strengths: Slide 1 establishes a tailored history-detective premise through the tax paper, folded map, and letter rather than opening with a battle scene.
Slides 3, 5, and 7 responsibly introduce multiple causes, unequal experiences, and the continuation of slavery without reducing the conflict to heroes versus villains.
Slide 6 turns the requested everyday objects into clear inquiry questions, and the pastel palette remains consistent and child-friendly.
The deck avoids violent imagery and labels the invented viewpoints on slide 5 as illustrative rather than real biographies.

issues.evidence: The object image visibly retains a gray checkerboard-like background inside its beige panel, making the generated asset look incompletely composited.
issues.fix: Export the object cluster with a clean transparent or solid background and let it occupy more of the panel.

issues.evidence: The third map card is cut off by the right edge; only part of its green shape and the label beginning “Rio G” are visible. The requested location sequence therefore cannot be read.
issues.fix: Fit all three nested-location panels inside the frame and use recognizable, labeled silhouettes for South America, Brazil, and Rio Grande do Sul.

issues.evidence: Both lower cause cards extend beyond the bottom edge. The imperial-government explanation is visibly truncated, and the political-future card also loses content.
issues.fix: Reduce card height and text, or use a fully visible two-by-two grid with projection-safe bottom margins.

issues.evidence: The central “1835–1845” label is clipped at the bottom. The numbered marker 2 represents the entire period rather than a distinct event, so the timeline reveals little beyond the two endpoints.
issues.fix: Move the timeline upward and add one or two meaningful midpoint events or child-centered changes instead of a redundant duration marker.

issues.evidence: The lower Rosa/Luzia/Davi/Tomás card row is cut off, preventing two viewpoints from being read. The people are represented by generic line icons rather than the requested illustrated characters.
issues.fix: Replace the card grid with four fully visible character illustrations and one short viewpoint sentence for each.

issues.evidence: The right-hand panel runs below the frame; the sentence about abolition is visibly cut off. This is a key historical conclusion and cannot be presented partially.
issues.fix: Shorten the two-column comparison and keep both conclusions fully within the slide.

issues.evidence: Only “Question 1 of 3” is visible, while the lower quiz content is cut off. The “Show the answer” and “Next question” controls look interactive but provide no visible answers or remaining questions in the rendered deck.
issues.fix: Present all three questions and their answer check within the static slide, or provide separate, fully rendered question and answer slides.

A.signatureMoment: Slide 1's three-object mystery is the deck's most memorable idea, but the visibly unfinished image compositing prevents it from becoming a polished opening.

strengths: Slide 1 delivers a memorable opening: the detective question, tactile paper objects, question marks, and dark-versus-light split create a clear visual premise.

Slide 5 supplies the required audience-specific illustrated characters and explicitly distinguishes the invented viewpoints from real biographies. The four images make differences in status and experience immediately legible.
Slide 6 uses illustrated everyday objects as evidence rather than decoration, pairing each reconstruction with a focused historical question.
Slide 7 is a strong substantive visual: the red thread reconnects the map, tax paper, letter, and food basket while the right side separates what changed from what did not.
Slide 8 closes with three different retrieval and comparison tasks plus a reflective question about missing voices, giving the lesson a more thoughtful ending than a single factual quiz.
The deck consistently avoids battle imagery and flags its schematic map and reconstructed or illustrative material.

issues.evidence: A stray label under the Rio Grande do Sul panel is forced into a vertical stack of letters reading approximately “storycenter” and runs to the bottom edge. This is the reported overflow and a visible generation defect.
issues.fix: Remove the stray text and rebuild the third panel with a clean state label and marker.

issues.evidence: The three geographic shapes are highly abstract blobs; Brazil and South America are not recognizable enough to teach spatial location without relying on the headings.
issues.fix: Use simplified but recognizable nested maps with the relevant area highlighted at each scale.

issues.evidence: The four cause cards are clear but relatively prose-heavy for the request for little text, and the source is only a generic institution name rather than a usable citation.
issues.fix: Reduce each explanation to one short line and add a complete source reference in notes or a compact footer.

issues.evidence: The timeline has a useful beginning, middle, and end, but the “long middle” remains a broad duration statement rather than showing a concrete event or lived change.
issues.fix: Add one carefully selected midpoint event or child-centered consequence while keeping the three-part simplicity.

issues.evidence: The answer strip appears on the same slide as the questions, so students can read the answers before attempting the quiz.
issues.fix: Reveal the check later or move it to a separate answer slide.

B.signatureMoment: Slide 7's red-thread reconstruction physically reconnects the evidence objects and converts the recurring motif into a clear historical conclusion.

result.reason: B is the deck to give the user after a mandatory repair to slide 2. It wins whether reviewed A-to-B or B-to-A; there is no order reversal. Both decks meet the eight-slide format, use child-friendly color, cover the Ragamuffin War, and avoid violent battle imagery, but A fails the hard readability gate on multiple slides and does not provide actual illustrated characters. B also has a hard as-rendered overflow defect on slide 2, so neither deck is fully ready without revision. B nevertheless earns its added visual complexity on slides 5–7 through explanatory character and object imagery, while A's complexity repeatedly produces clipped cards and an incomplete quiz. Route identity is unavailable, so no claim can be made about which arm was the original. The single most useful change to A would be rebuilding its layout system around fixed safe margins so every map, viewpoint, conclusion, and quiz item renders inside the frame. B exceeds competent default quality in its object-based narrative and viewpoint sequence, but the broken map slide and several conventional card layouts keep it from exceptional or sustained-wow status.
result.whatWouldMakeWinnerExceptional: Replace slide 2 with a polished, recognizable nested-map journey from South America to Brazil to Rio Grande do Sul, with no overflow and minimal labels; this would remove the blocking defect and give the strong opening a genuinely explanatory visual payoff.
